# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–25 (Complete – Updated 176)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Spring of seventh year** (Chapter 25). Major Dobbin has arrived in England and reunited with Amelia. Rawdon governs Coventry Island (winter of sixth year). Georgy established at Russell Square with grandfather.
- **Key temporal markers**: Chapter 24 opened "winter of sixth year"; Chapter 25 opens "spring of seventh year."
- **Locations**: London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Gaunt House, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks, Russell Square, Brompton, Conduit Street, Hart Street Bloomsbury, Southampton Row, Kensington Gardens, Camberwell, Slaughters' Inn); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe hill farms; Bryngate market town; Piccadilly; Madras (India); St. Helena; Cape; Southampton; Belgium (Brussels, Mount St. John); Bengal; various English countryside towns.

## The Duel Resolution and Its Immediate Aftermath (Chapter 23–24)

**Macmurdo's Intervention (Chapter 23)**: When Rawdon wavered after learning of Coventry Island appointment, Macmurdo rebuked him, insisting affair was placed in his hands. Refused to carry further challenge; argued duel would disgrace all parties. Advised Rawdon to accept position and maintain silence.

**Duel Occurred (Chapter 24)**: Secret rencontre between Rawdon and Steyne; principals and seconds agreed to bury outcome "in the profoundest oblivion." Despite sworn secrecy, story spread rapidly across London within hours. **Scandal suppressed from newspapers by Mr. Wagg acting on Wenham's hint**—kept from press.

**Rawdon's Refusal of Reconciliation (Chapter 24)**: Rawdon refused Pitt's reconciliation message. Rebecca concealed money from him ten years; she swore she had none from Steyne, but "directly I found it" she knew "it was all up." Rawdon declared: "If she's not guilty, Pitt, she's as bad as guilty, and I'll never see her again--never."

**Rawdon's Acceptance of Governorship (Chapter 24)**: Initially resisted appointment "procured for him by so odious a patron" (Steyne). Persuaded to accept by Pitt's entreaties and mainly Macmurdo's argument that accepting position would spite Steyne by making him instrument of Rawdon's prosperity.

## Rebecca's Final Dissolution (Chapter 24)

**Household Seized**: Bailiffs seized Raggles's property in Curzon Street. Rebecca's fate immediately after unknown—"where? Who cared!"

**Financial Arrangements**: Rawdon made Rebecca "tolerable annuity"—she possessed talent for "making a little money go a great way."

## Rawdon's Life in Coventry Island (Chapter 24)

**Colonial Governance**: Governor of Coventry Island, three thousand a year. Maintains honor, fulfills obligations, provides for son's education and future, compensates those wronged (Briggs via Pitt). Complete moral transformation accomplished.

## Georgy Osborne's Establishment and Education (Chapter 24)

**Current Status**: "Fairly established in his grandfather's mansion in Russell Square, occupant of his father's room...and heir apparent of all the splendours there." Mr. Osborne "as proud of him as ever he had been of the elder George"—boy's "good looks, gallant bearing, and gentlemanlike appearance" won grandsire's heart.

**Intellectual Superiority**: Georgy's superior education made him "a much better gentleman" than grandfather's plans. Boy's "quick brain and better education" showed grandfather was "a dullard." Boy began "accordingly to command him and to look down upon him."

**Physical Appearance and Dress**: Scarcely eleven years old; wore straps, beautiful little boots, gilt spurs, gold-headed whip. Dressed for dinner daily "like a regular West End swell." One domestic specially attended him.

**Daily Habits**: After breakfast, sat reading Morning Post "just like a grown-up man." Made house lively "by his activity, his imperiousness, his scolding, and his good-nature." Domineer[s] over everybody; "in Russell Square, everybody was afraid of Mr. Osborne, and Mr. Osborne was afraid of Georgy."

**Friendships**: Young Todd of Coram Street was Master George's great friend. Both attended principal theatres; knew names of all actors. **Mrs. Todd's private plan (rumor)**: Noted Georgy and her youngest daughter Rosa Jemima "looked so well together" and privately wondered "who knows what might happen?"

**Reverend Lawrence Veal's School** (Hart Street, Bloomsbury): Veal is domestic Chaplain to Earl of Bareacres. Georgy is day boy only, arrives mornings under Rowson's guardianship, rides away afternoons on pony. **Notable failing**: Veal frequently tolerates Georgy's late arrival and defaulting behavior without consequences. Marked: aristos in Greek, optimus in Latin, très bien in French.

**Amelia's Involvement with School**: Made friends with Mrs. Veal "for reasons of her own." Attended Mrs. Veal's monthly conversazioni with pink cards. Walked from Brompton "in any weather" and embraced Mrs. Veal "with tearful gratitude."

**Emotional Indifference**: Georgy bears separation from Amelia easily, whilst "his mother was yearning after him at home...every hour of the day."

## Amelia's Captivity and Suffering (Chapter 24)

**Mrs. Sedley's Death**: Few months after Georgy began with paternal grandfather, Mrs. Sedley died. "There had been little love between her and the child. He did not care to show much grief. He came down to visit his mother in a fine new suit of mourning, and was very angry that he could not go to a play." Amelia had smoothed pillow; soothed sufferer with words of hope; "closed the eyes that had once looked so tenderly upon her."

**John Sedley's Destitution**: Old man "stunned by the blow which had befallen him." "There was only Amelia to stand by and support with her gentle arms the tottering, heart-broken old man."

**Financial Dependence on Osborne**: "One of the many causes for personal pride with which old Osborne chose to recreate himself that Sedley...was in his last days so utterly defeated and humiliated as to be forced to accept pecuniary obligations at the hands of the man who had most injured and insulted him." Osborne "cursed the old pauper and relieved him from time to time."

**Amelia's Acceptance and Prison**: Her life "had come down to this--to a mean prison and a long, ignoble bondage." Russell Square was "the boundary of her prison: she might walk thither occasionally, but was always back to sleep in her cell at night."

**Amelia's Devotion**: She determined "with all her might and strength to try and make her old father happy. She slaved, toiled, patched, and mended, sang and played backgammon, read out the newspaper, cooked dishes for old Sedley, walked him out sedulously into Kensington Gardens or the Brompton Lanes, listened to his stories with untiring smiles and affectionate hypocrisy."

**Miniature Portrait**: Georgy commissioned miniature of himself, paying from own money. Old Osborne, pleased, gave boy twice the sovereigns paid. Amelia hung portrait beside another miniature over her bed. Slept with picture under pillow; kissed and wept and prayed over it "many many times." "Since her parting with George she had had no such joy and consolation."

## Major Dobbin's Return and Journey Home (Chapter 24–25)

**Illness in Madras**: Major Dobbin obtained leave, travelled "night and day until he reached his journey's end." Arrived at Madras "in a high fever." Servants brought him to friend's house "in a state of delirium"; thought for many days he would not travel farther than "the burying-ground of the church of St. George's."

**Delirium and Testament**: During fever, "the poor fellow lay tossing in his fever...raving about Amelia." Made solemn preparations, leaving "the little property of which he was possessed to those whom he most desired to benefit." "He desired to be buried with a little brown hair-chain which he wore round his neck and which...he had got from Amelia's maid at Brussels, when the young widow's hair was cut off, during the fever which prostrated her after the death of George Osborne on the plateau at Mount St. John."

**Recovery and Passage on Ramchunder**: Dobbin recovered and took passage with Jos Sedley. After passing St. Helena, displayed "gaiety and strength" astonishing to fellow passengers. Became "so impatient and ill-humoured" within ten days' sail of England, recovered when breeze sprang up. "Good God, how his heart beat as the two friendly spires of Southampton came in sight."

**Landing and Journey Inland**: Entire crew gave three cheers for Major Dobbin at landing. Jos, "who very likely thought the cheers were for himself, took off his gold-laced cap and waved it majestically." They proceeded to Royal George Hotel. Dobbin made early departure next morning, "obliged to retreat, leaving Jos to resume his interrupted slumbers."

**Rapid Journey to London**: Travelled rapidly "as if he had been an English nobleman travelling on a pleasure tour." Post-boys wondered at fees. Passed "through neat country towns...by old halls and parks; rustic hamlets clustered round ancient grey churches--and through the charming friendly English landscape." At Slaughters' Inn, inquired about "Captain Osborne's widow"; innkeeper John noted loan from April 1815. Dobbin "chose out of his kit the very smartest and most becoming civil costume he possessed, and laughed at his own tanned face and grey hair."

**Reunion with Clapps and Binny (Chapter 25)**: Dobbin called at Clapp's house in Brompton. Was greeted by Miss Mary Polly Clapp. Identified himself as "an old friend," Georgy's godfather, "just come back from India." Proposed Polly guide him to Amelia; she "bounced away to her apartment and appeared presently in her best bonnet and her mamma's yellow shawl."

**Encounter with Reverend Binny (Chapter 25)**: During walk with Polly, "a pale young man with feeble whiskers and a stiff white neckcloth came walking down the lane, en sandwich--having a lady, that is, on each arm." Polly identified: "That is our curate, the Reverend Mr. Binny...and his sister Miss B....and the other lady, the little one with a cast in her eye and the handsome watch, is Mrs. Binny--Miss Grits that was; her pa was a grocer...They were married last month, and are just come back from Margate. She's five thousand pound to her fortune." Dobbin twitched, "slapped the bamboo on the ground with an emphasis which made Miss Clapp cry, 'Law,' and laugh too." He stood "silent, with open mouth, looking after the retreating young couple," but "did not hear beyond the announcement of the reverend gentleman's marriage; his head was swimming with felicity." Began walking "double quick towards the place of his destination...through the Brompton lanes, and entering at the little old portal in Kensington Garden wall."

**Meeting with Amelia (Chapter 25)**: "Old Sedley was seated on a bench, his handkerchief placed over his knees, prattling away, according to his wont, with some old story about old times." When Mary appeared, "Amelia caught sight of her, she started up from her bench. Her first thought was that something had happened to Georgy, but the sight of the messenger's eager and happy face dissipated that fear." Dobbin's "lean figure and long shadow stalking across the grass" caused Amelia to start, blush, and cry. She came "running towards him, her hands before her, ready to give them to him." "She wasn't changed. She was a little pale, a little stouter in figure. Her eyes were the same, the kind trustful eyes. There were scarce three lines of silver in her soft brown hair." He took "the two little hands between his two and held them there. He was speechless for a moment. Why did he not take her in his arms and swear that he would never leave her? She must have yielded: she could not but have obeyed him."

**Tea at Sedley's Home (Chapter 25)**: Although "he had such particular business in London that evening," Dobbin consented to forego it upon Mr. Sedley's invitation to tea. "Amelia put her arm under that of her young friend with the yellow shawl and headed the party on their return homewards, so that Mr. Sedley fell to Dobbin's share." Old man "walked very slowly and told a number of ancient histories about himself and his poor Bessy, his former prosperity, and his bankruptcy." Dobbin's "eyes were fixed upon the figure in front of him--the dear little figure always present to his imagination and in his prayers, and visiting his dreams wakeful or slumbering."

**Amelia's Hospitality (Chapter 25)**: "Amelia was very happy, smiling, and active all that evening, performing her duties as hostess of the little entertainment with the utmost grace and propriety, as Dobbin thought. His eyes followed her about as they sat in the twilight." He had "longed for that moment and thought of her far away under hot winds and in weary marches, gentle and happy, kindly ministering to the wants of old age, and decorating poverty with sweet submission--as he saw her now."

**Amelia Encourages Tea (Chapter 25)**: "Amelia seeing this propensity, laughingly encouraged it and looked exceedingly roguish as she administered to him cup after cup." She did not know "that the Major had had no dinner and that the cloth was laid for him at the Slaughters', and a plate laid thereon to mark that the table was retained, in that very box in which the Major and George had sat many a time carousing, when she was a child just come home from Miss Pinkerton's school."

**Georgy's Miniature (Chapter 25)**: "The first thing Mrs. Osborne showed the Major was Georgy's miniature, for which she ran upstairs on her arrival at home. It was not half handsome enough of course for the boy, but wasn't it noble of him to think of bringing it to his mother? Whilst her papa was awake she did not talk much about Georgy. To hear about Mr. Osborne and Russell Square was not agreeable to the old man, who very likely was unconscious that he had been living for some months past mainly on the bounty of his richer rival, and lost his temper if allusion was made to the other."

**Dobbin's Conversation with Jos (Chapter 25)**: "Dobbin told him all, and a little more perhaps than all, that had happened on board the Ramchunder, and exaggerated Jos's benevolent dispositions towards his father and resolution to make him comfortable in his old days. The truth is that during the voyage the Major had impressed this duty most strongly upon his fellow-passenger and extorted promises from him that he would take charge of his sister and her child."

**Dobbin's Hesitation and Departure (Chapter 25)**: When pressed to stay "to-morrow," Dobbin demurred: "Not to-morrow...I have business." He did not like to own "that he had not as yet been to his parents' and his dear sister Anne--a remissness for which I am sure every well-regulated person will blame the Major." He took his leave, leaving his address for Jos. "And so the first day was over, and he had seen her. When he got back to the Slaughters', the roast fowl was of course cold, in which condition he ate it for supper...Major Dobbin treated himself to half-price at the Haymarket Theatre that evening, where let us hope he enjoyed himself."

**Dobbin's Internal Conflict (Chapter 25)**: As holding Amelia's hand, "Ought I to be angry with her for being faithful to him?...Ought I to be jealous of my friend in the grave, or hurt that such a heart as Amelia's can love only once and for ever? Oh, George, George, how little you knew the prize you had, though." This sentiment "passed rapidly through William's mind."

## Jos Sedley's Return (Chapter 24–25)

**Ten Years in Bengal**: Jos had passed ten years in Bengal. "Constant dinners, tiffins, pale ale and claret, the prodigious labour of cutcherry, and the refreshment of brandy-pawnee which he was forced to take there, had their effect upon Waterloo Sedley." Having served full time with fine appointments, he laid by considerable money and was free to return to Europe with good pension.

**Passage on Ramchunder (Chapter 24–25)**: After leaving St. Helena, became "very generous, disposing of a great quantity of ship stores." No ladies on board; Jos was "the first dignitary at table." Disappeared "rather in a panic during a two-days' gale," remained in cot reading *The Washerwoman of Finchley Common*.

**Conversations with Dobbin**: "Many and many a night as the ship was cutting through the roaring dark sea...Mr. Sedley and the Major would sit on the quarter-deck of the vessel talking about home, as the Major smoked his cheroot."
